II. The Preamble describes India as Democratic.
III. The Preamble describes India as a Republic.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

3.s:
How many of the following statements correctly describe concepts associated with the Preamble?

2. Democracy means government of the people.

3.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949 and enacted it on the same date.
Statement B: According to the Preamble, the people of India give the Constitution to themselves.

Which of the following is correct?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
3.x: Both are true: the Preamble says 'We, the people of India … do hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution' on 26 November 1949, so the people are its source.
3.tq: Read the Preamble's closing words: adopt, enact and give to ourselves.

3.s: Which one of the following correctly describes a republic?
o: It does not have a hereditary head of state
It has a hereditary head of state
It excludes the idea of an elected head of state
It is governed only by external authority
3.x: A republic has an elected head of State, not a hereditary one. Options B and C describe monarchy, and D contradicts sovereignty.
n: A republic does not have a hereditary head of state. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 36-38]

3.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Justice in the Preamble includes social, economic and political justice.
II. Liberty in the Preamble concerns thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
III. Equality in the Preamble concerns status and opportunity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
3.x: All three are correct: justice is social, economic and political; liberty is of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; equality is of status and opportunity.

3.s: Which case held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution?
3.x: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution, overruling Berubari (1960), which had said it was not; LIC of India (1995) reaffirmed this. Golaknath (1967) dealt with amending Fundamental Rights.
3.tq: Link 'Preamble is part of the Constitution' to the basic-structure case.
n: The Golaknath Case held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 36-38]

Statement A is true, Statement B is false

3.x: Both are true: the Preamble is called the key to the Constitution and its soul.
3.tq: Recall the descriptions given to the Preamble.

The Preamble is called the Soul of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 36-38]

3.s: Who called the Preamble the “Political Horoscope”?
3.x: K.M. Munshi called the Preamble the 'Political Horoscope' of the Constitution. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul', and Hidayatullah called the Preamble its soul.
3.tq: Match each description to the person who gave it.
n: K. M. Munshi called the Preamble the Political Horoscope. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 36-38]

3.s: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act is popularly known as the:
3.x: The 42nd Amendment (1976) is called the 'Mini Constitution' because of its sweeping changes. 'Soul' and 'key' describe the Preamble and 'political horoscope' is Munshi's phrase for it.

n: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act is known as the Mini Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 36-38]

4.s: The constitutional provisions relating to citizenship are primarily contained in which Part and Articles of the Constitution?
4.x: Citizenship is in Part II, Articles 5–11, which identifies citizens at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950). Part III (12–35) is Fundamental Rights and Part I (1–4) the Union and its territory.
4.tq: Link citizenship to Part II.

4.s: Under Article 5, which of the following is one of the conditions connected with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution?
o: Residence in India for at least 5 years prior to 1950
Registration with the Election Commission before 1950
Residence in India for at least 2 years prior to 1950
Ownership of property in India before 1950
4.x: Article 5 conferred citizenship on persons domiciled in India who were born in India, had a parent born in India, or had lived in India for at least five years before 1950. Two years and property ownership are distractors.

5.s: Part III of the Constitution, containing the Fundamental Rights, is rightly described as the:
5.x: Part III is called the Magna Carta of India because it guarantees basic civil liberties against the State. "Instrument of Instructions" describes the Directive Principles, and Fundamental Duties act as a code for citizens.
5.tq: Link each part of the Constitution to its well-known description.
n: Part III contains 24 Articles. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]

5.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Article 19 provides eight grounds of reasonable restriction for freedom of speech and expression.
Statement B: Freedom of peaceful assembly can be restricted in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India and public order.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
5.x: Both are true: Article 19(2) lists eight grounds for restricting speech, and Article 19(3) allows restrictions on assembly for sovereignty and integrity of India and public order.
5.tq: Remember speech has the most grounds of restriction.
n: Article 19 provides eight grounds of reasonable restriction for speech. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Other freedoms under Article 19 have three to four grounds of reasonable restriction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]

5.s:
Assertion (A): The maximum period of preventive detention without an advisory board is three months.
Reason (R): Article 22 specifies the three-month maximum period of preventive detention without an advisory board.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
5.x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 22 limits preventive detention without an Advisory Board's report to three months.
5.tq: Check whether R is the source of the limit.
n: The maximum period of preventive detention without an advisory board is three months. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Article 22 specifies the three-month maximum period of preventive detention without an advisory board. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]

5.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Fundamental Rights other than those under Articles 20 and 21 may be suspended by a Presidential Order under Article 359.
II. Articles 20 and 21 are excepted from suspension by a Presidential Order under Article 359.
III. Articles 20 and 21 are included among the Fundamental Rights that may be suspended under Article 359.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
5.x: I and II are correct: under Article 359 the President can suspend enforcement of Fundamental Rights except Articles 20 and 21. III contradicts II.
5.tq: Remember 20 and 21 cannot be suspended.
n: Fundamental Rights other than those under Articles 20 and 21 may be suspended by a Presidential Order under Article 359. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Articles 20 and 21 are excepted from suspension by a Presidential Order under Article 359. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]

5.s: Which Articles of the Constitution empower the Supreme Court and High Courts to issue writs?
5.x: The Supreme Court issues writs under Article 32 and High Courts under Article 226. Article 136 is special leave to appeal, not writ power. Option C reverses the order.
5.tq: Match 'respectively' to the right order.
n: The Supreme Court issues writs under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
High Courts issue writs under Article 226. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s: Why did Dr. B.R. Ambedkar describe Article 32 as the “heart and soul of the Constitution”?
o: It empowers the President to issue constitutional writs
It guarantees a direct and effective Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies
It gives Parliament power to amend Fundamental Rights
It establishes the jurisdiction of High Courts over statutory rights
5.x: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution because it makes the right to a remedy itself a Fundamental Right, giving direct access to the Supreme Court.
5.tq: Link the description to the guaranteed remedy.
n: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar designated Article 32 as the “heart and soul of the Constitution.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Article 32 guarantees a direct and effective Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s: Which writ is primarily used to compel performance of a mandatory public or legal duty that has been refused or neglected?
5.x: Mandamus ('we command') orders a public authority to perform a duty it has refused or neglected. Prohibition stops a court, Quo Warranto questions a title to office, Habeas Corpus frees a detainee.
5.tq: Link 'perform a duty' to Mandamus.
n: Mandamus compels performance of a mandatory public or legal duty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus applies when a mandatory public or legal duty has been refused or neglected. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Supreme Court may issue writs under Article 32 only for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
The High Courts have a narrower writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court.
Article 32 is connected with the Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies.
The High Courts may issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose.
5.x: B is incorrect: High Courts have wider writ power, because under Article 226 they can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and 'any other purpose'; the Supreme Court under Article 32 only for Fundamental Rights.
5.tq: Check which court's power is wider.
n: The Supreme Court has narrower writ jurisdiction under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
The Supreme Court issues writs only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights in Part III. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
The High Courts have wider writ jurisdiction under Article 226. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
The High Courts issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
The High Courts issue writs for any other purpose, including enforcement of ordinary statutory or legal rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Habeas Corpus?
o: It may be directed against public authorities and private individuals.
It is used only against public authorities and cannot lie against private individuals.
It is applicable whenever detention is illegal.
5.x: B is incorrect: Habeas Corpus lies against both public authorities and private individuals who detain a person illegally — it is the only writ available against private persons.
5.tq: Remember Habeas Corpus reaches private detainers.
n: Habeas Corpus targets public authorities. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Habeas Corpus targets private individuals. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Habeas Corpus safeguards individual liberty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Habeas Corpus applies whenever detention is illegal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Mandamus?
o: It can compel performance of a mandatory public or legal duty.
It lies against the President and Governors for every refused public duty.
It may lie against a government company performing a public function.
5.x: B is incorrect: Mandamus does not lie against the President or Governors (or private bodies without public duties). It can lie against government companies performing public functions.
5.tq: Recall who is immune from Mandamus.
n: Mandamus literally means “We command.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus compels performance of a mandatory public or legal duty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus does not lie against the President or Governors. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus can lie against a government company performing a public function. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s:
Assertion (A): Prohibition is a preventive writ.
Reason (R): It is issued after an inferior court has passed its final order to quash that order.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
5.x: A is true, R is false: Prohibition is preventive — issued while proceedings are pending to stop a court exceeding jurisdiction. Quashing a final order is done by Certiorari.
5.tq: Separate preventive Prohibition from curative Certiorari.
n: Prohibition is issued while the proceeding is still pending in the lower body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari quashes an illegal order already passed. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari is issued after an order or decision is made. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Prohibition operates while a judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding is pending. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari is issued to correct or quash an order. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s:
Assertion (A): Any member of the public can move a petition for Quo-Warranto.
Reason (R): Quo-Warranto literally means "by what authority or warrant".
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
5.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the literal meaning of Quo Warranto does not explain why any public-spirited person, not only an aggrieved one, may seek it.
5.tq: Purpose of a writ does not explain who may file it.
n: Quo-Warranto targets a person holding a substantive public office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Quo-Warranto targets a person claiming a substantive public office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Any public-minded citizen can move a Quo-Warranto petition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Quo-Warranto challenges the legal qualification or title of a person holding public office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Any member of the public can file a Quo-Warranto petition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 32 gives the Supreme Court writ jurisdiction for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
II. Article 226 enables High Courts to issue writs for ordinary statutory or legal rights as well.
III. Article 32(3) permits Parliament to empower any other court to exercise, within its local jurisdiction, all or any powers exercisable by the Supreme Court.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
5.x: All three are correct: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court writ power for Fundamental Rights, Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for legal rights too, and Article 32(3) lets Parliament empower other courts locally.
5.tq: Check each clause of Articles 32 and 226.
n: The Supreme Court issues writs only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights in Part III. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Habeas Corpus is a remedy for illegal custody of a person.
Statement B: Mandamus is a remedy for non-performance of a legal duty by a public authority.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
5.x: Both are true: Habeas Corpus is the remedy for illegal custody, and Mandamus for a public authority's failure to perform a legal duty.

n: Habeas Corpus targets illegal custody of a person. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Habeas Corpus provides a remedy for bodily freedom. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus targets non-performance of a legal duty by a public authority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Mandamus and Quo-Warranto have the same core objective.
Statement B: Quo-Warranto requires the petitioner to be personally aggrieved.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
5.x: Both are false: Mandamus commands performance of a public duty, while Quo Warranto tests a person's right to hold a public office; and Quo Warranto can be filed by any citizen, without personal injury.
5.tq: Check the purpose and the locus standi of each writ.
n: Quo-Warranto does not require aggrieved-party status. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

5.s:

2. Mandamus can lie against a government company performing a public function.
3. Prohibition is issued after an order has been passed.
4. Certiorari is issued after an order or decision has been made.
5.x: Three are correct: Habeas Corpus can lie against a private person, Mandamus against a government company doing public work, and Certiorari after an order is made. Statement 3 is wrong — Prohibition is issued while proceedings are still pending.
5.tq: Check the timing of each writ.
n: Habeas Corpus can lie against private persons. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Prohibition is issued while the proceeding is still pending in the lower body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari is issued after an order or decision is made. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]

A Governor acting in the discharge of office
A government company or statutory corporation

11.x: Both are true: under Article 312, the Rajya Sabha can start the creation of a new All-India Service by a two-thirds resolution, and it is a permanent House. Its permanence is not the basis of the Article 312 power, so R does not explain A.

n: The Rajya Sabha can initiate the creation of new All-India Services under Article 312. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]

11.s:

11.tq: Remember that only Money Bills limit the Rajya Sabha's role.
n: The Rajya Sabha has equal powers with the Lok Sabha in Constitutional Amendment Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The Rajya Sabha can introduce Ordinary Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The Rajya Sabha can introduce Constitutional Amendment Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]

11.s: How many of the following statements regarding Lok Sabha membership are correct? I. The minimum age for Lok Sabha membership is 25 years. II. The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is 550 members. III. The Lok Sabha is elected directly. IV. The term of a Lok Sabha member is five years.
11.x: All four are correct: the minimum age is 25, the maximum strength is 550 (530 from States and 20 from UTs) since Anglo-Indian nomination ended, election is direct, and the term is five years.
11.tq: Check each Lok Sabha number: 25, 552 and five years.
n: The minimum age for Lok Sabha membership is 25 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is 552 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The Lok Sabha is elected directly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The term of a Lok Sabha member is five years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]

11.s:
How many of the following statements regarding the Lok Sabha are correct?

II. The Lok Sabha has no nominated members.
III. Anglo-Indian nomination to the Lok Sabha has been abolished.

n: The Lok Sabha can be dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The Lok Sabha has no nominated members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
Anglo-Indian nomination to the Lok Sabha has been abolished. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]

11.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Rajya Sabha’s role in relation to a Money Bill is incorrect?
o: It must deal with a Money Bill within 14 days.
Its role is limited to recommending changes to the Money Bill.
It can only recommend changes to a Money Bill.
It introduces the Money Bill and has the final say on it.
11.x: Option D is incorrect. A Money Bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha, which also has the final say; the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days.
11.tq: Discriminate the roles of the two Houses on Money Bills.
n: The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes to a Money Bill within 14 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]

11.s:
Assertion (A): The Lok Sabha introduces Money Bills and has the final say on them.
Reason (R): The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes to a Money Bill within 14 days.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
11.x: Both are true: the Lok Sabha introduces Money Bills and has the final say, and the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days. The Rajya Sabha's limited role is why the Lok Sabha's word is final, so R explains A.
11.tq: Ask whether R's limit on one House accounts for A's power of the other.
n: The Lok Sabha introduces Money Bills and has the final say on them. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]

11.tq: Pair the Union and State versions: 74 with 163, and 80 with 168 to 171.

11.s:

n: The Union Council of Ministers is collectively responsible strictly to the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]

The Union Council of Ministers is not collectively responsible to the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]

The Council of Ministers is not collectively responsible to the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]

11.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Union Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President.
Union Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Prime Minister.
State Ministers do not hold office during the pleasure of the Chief Minister.
State Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Governor.
11.x: Option B is incorrect. Union Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, not the Prime Minister. State Ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure, not the Chief Minister's.

11.s:
Consider the following statements:

II. The State Council of Ministers cannot exceed 15% of the strength of the Legislative Assembly.
III. The minimum number of Ministers in a State Council of Ministers is 12.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
11.x: All three are correct: the 91st Amendment, 2003 caps the Union ministry at 15% of the Lok Sabha and a State ministry at 15% of the Assembly, and a State ministry must have at least 12 Ministers.
11.tq: Recall the 91st Amendment's 15 per cent cap and the minimum of 12.
n: The maximum size of the Union Council of Ministers is 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha under the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]

The maximum size of the State Council of Ministers is 15% of the strength of the Legislative Assembly under the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The State Council of Ministers must have at least 12 ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]

11.s: A person who is not a member of Parliament may remain a Union Minister for a maximum period of:
11.x: Under Article 75(5), a non-member can be a Union Minister for at most six consecutive months. The same six-month limit applies to State Ministers under Article 164(4).
11.tq: Recall the six-month window for non-member Ministers.
n: A person who is not a member of Parliament can remain a Union Minister for a maximum of six consecutive months under Article 75(5). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]

The Union Cabinet consists of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The State Cabinet is the inner core consisting of the Chief Minister and Cabinet Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]

11.s:

o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

11.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Council of States is incorrect?

11.s:

II. The Legislative Assembly is the final authority in relation to a Money Bill.
III. The Legislative Council has only a recommendatory role in relation to a Money Bill.
IV. The Legislative Council may retain a Money Bill for a maximum of one month.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
11.x: I, II and III are correct: a Money Bill starts only in the Assembly, which has the final say, while the Council can only make recommendations. IV is false because the Council can hold a Money Bill for at most 14 days, not a month.
11.tq: Discriminate the 14-day Money Bill limit from the ordinary-Bill delays.
n: The Legislative Assembly is the sole House of introduction for a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The Legislative Assembly has final authority over a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]

11.s: The provisions relating to State Legislatures are contained in which Part and range of Articles of the Constitution?
11.x: Part VI, Articles 168–212, covers State Legislatures. Part V, Articles 79–122, covers Parliament.
11.tq: Discriminate Part V (Union) from Part VI (States).
n: Indian State legislatures are governed under Part VI of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Part VI contains Articles 168 to 212 concerning Indian State legislatures. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: A bicameral State Legislature consists of the Governor, Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council.
Statement B: A unicameral State Legislature consists of the Governor and Legislative Assembly.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
11.x: Both are true: under Article 168, a bicameral State Legislature has the Governor, Assembly and Council, and a unicameral one has the Governor and Assembly. The Governor is part of both.
11.tq: Remember that the Governor is part of every State Legislature.
n: A bicameral State legislature consists of the Governor, the Legislative Assembly, and the Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
A unicameral State legislature consists of the Governor and the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s: Which State has the largest Legislative Council, with 100 seats?
11.x: Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council, with 100 seats, among the six bicameral States.
11.tq: Recall the largest of the six State Legislative Councils.
n: Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council, with 100 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
India currently has 6 bicameral States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Uttar Pradesh is a bicameral State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s: Bicameralism was first introduced in India at the Central level by which enactment?
11.x: The Government of India Act, 1919 first brought bicameralism to the Centre, with the Council of State and Central Legislative Assembly. The 1935 Act brought it to some provinces.
11.tq: Discriminate the 1919 Act (Centre) from the 1935 Act (provinces).
n: Bicameralism was first introduced in India at the Central level by the Government of India Act, 1919. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Government of India Act, 1919, created the Council of State and the Central Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

o: The State Legislative Council is a permanent body and cannot be dissolved.
The State Legislative Council cannot be abolished because it is a permanent body.
One-third of the Council members retire every two years.
The State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169.
11.x: Option B is incorrect. The Council is permanent, so it cannot be dissolved, but it can be abolished under Article 169. One-third of its members retire every two years.
11.tq: Discriminate between dissolving a House and abolishing it.

The State Legislative Council cannot be dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

The Council of States cannot be dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The maximum strength of a State Legislative Council is one-third of the strength of the Legislative Assembly.
II. The minimum strength of a State Legislative Council is 40.
III. The maximum strength of a Legislative Assembly is 500 and its minimum strength is 60.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
11.x: All three are correct: a Council can have at most one-third of the Assembly's strength and at least 40 members, and an Assembly has at most 500 and at least 60 members.
11.tq: Recall the four limits: 1/3, 40, 500 and 60.
n: The maximum size of a State Legislative Council is one-third of the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The minimum size of a State Legislative Council is 40 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The maximum size of a State Legislative Assembly is 500 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The minimum size of a State Legislative Assembly is 60 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s: Who presides over the State Legislative Council?
o: The Chairman elected by the Council from among its members
The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
11.x: Under Article 182, the Council elects its Chairman from among its own members. The Governor does not nominate the Chairman, and the Vice-President chairs only the Rajya Sabha.
11.tq: Discriminate the Council's Chairman from the Rajya Sabha's ex-officio Chairman.
n: The Chairman of the State Legislative Council is elected by the Council from among its members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Chairman of the Legislative Council is chosen by the Council members from among themselves under Article 182. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Governor does not nominate the Chairman of the Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s:
Assertion (A): Creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
Reason (R): Parliament enacts the law for creation or abolition of a Legislative Council by a simple majority.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
11.x: Both are true: Parliament passes the law by simple majority, and the Constitution itself says such a law is not an amendment under Article 368. R explains how the law is passed, not why it is excluded from Article 368.
11.tq: Ask whether the type of majority explains the Article 368 exclusion.
n: Parliament passes the law for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council by a simple majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Creation or abolition of a Legislative Council is not considered an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Parliament enacts the law for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The parliamentary law for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council is passed like an ordinary bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s: Which of the following statements regarding a State Assembly resolution for creation or abolition of a Legislative Council is incorrect?
o: It must be passed by a special majority.
It legally compels the Union Government to introduce a Bill in Parliament.
At least two-thirds of the members present and voting must support it.
At least 50% of the total membership must support it.
11.x: Option B is incorrect: the Assembly's resolution is only a request and does not legally compel the Union Government to bring a Bill. It does need a special majority (50% of total membership and two-thirds present and voting).
11.tq: Look for the statement that makes a recommendation binding.
n: The State Legislative Assembly resolution for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council requires a special majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The special majority requires at least 50 percent of the total membership of the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The special majority requires at least two-thirds of the members present and voting in the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Assembly resolution for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council is recommendatory. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Assembly resolution does not legally compel the Union Government to introduce a bill in Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Assembly initiates the creation or abolition of a Legislative Council by passing a resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s: Elections to the State Legislative Council are conducted by which voting method?
o: Proportional Representation by means of Single Transferable Vote under secret ballot
Direct election by all adult residents under secret ballot
Proportional Representation by list system under open ballot
11.x: Council elections use proportional representation by single transferable vote, by secret ballot, as Rajya Sabha elections do. First-past-the-post and open ballot are distractors.
11.tq: Recall that indirect elections use the single transferable vote.
n: Elections to a State Legislative Council use proportional representation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Elections to a State Legislative Council use the single transferable vote system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The single transferable vote system for State Legislative Council elections is conducted by secret ballot. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

Industrialists are not valid nomination categories for a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Governor’s five nomination fields for a State Legislative Council are literature, science, art, the co-operative movement, and social service. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s: A Money Bill in a State Legislature can originate only in which House?
o: A joint sitting of both Houses
Either House at the discretion of the Governor

n: A Money Bill can originate only in the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Legislative Council must return a Money Bill with its recommendations within 14 days.
Statement B: If the Council does not return the Money Bill within 14 days, the Bill is deemed to have been passed on the expiry of that period.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
11.x: Both are true: the Council can only make recommendations on a Money Bill and must return it within 14 days. If it does not, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses.
11.tq: Recall the 14-day limit and the deemed-passed rule.
n: The Legislative Council receives a Money Bill only for recommendations. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council must return a Money Bill within 14 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
A Money Bill is deemed to have been passed upon expiry of 14 days if the Legislative Council does not return it. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s:
Consider the following statements about an ordinary Bill passed by the Legislative Assembly:
I. The Legislative Council can delay it for a maximum of three months on the first passage.
II. After the Assembly repasses it, the Council can delay it for a maximum of one month.
III. The Council can permanently block the legislation by exercising a veto.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
11.x: I and II are correct: the Council can delay an ordinary Bill for three months, then one month after it is passed again. III is false because the Council has no veto.
11.tq: Find the statement giving the Council a veto.
n: The Legislative Council has no veto power over ordinary bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council cannot permanently block legislation passed by the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill for a maximum of 3 months after its first passage. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council can delay a re-passed ordinary bill for a maximum of 1 month. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Assembly can re-pass an ordinary bill after its first passage through the Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

The State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169, whereas the Rajya Sabha cannot be abolished.
11.x: A State Legislative Council, though permanent, can be abolished under Article 169. The Rajya Sabha cannot be abolished, which is the difference.

n: The State Legislative Council can be abolished. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Council of States cannot be abolished. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Council of States is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council cannot be dissolved on the recommendation of the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.x: The Legislative Council is permanent but can be abolished under Article 169, the Council of States is permanent and cannot be abolished, and the Assembly has a five-year term unless dissolved earlier. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
11.tq: Match the odd one out, the five-year Assembly, first.
n: Members of the State Legislative Council have a 6-year term. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
One-third of the members of the State Legislative Council retire every 2 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

One-third of the members of the Council of States retire every 2 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Members of the State Legislative Assembly have a 5-year term unless the Assembly is dissolved earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The normal term of the State Legislative Assembly is 5 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Assembly can be dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the composition of a State Legislative Council?
o: One-sixth of its members are nominated by the Governor.
One-fourth of its members are nominated by the Governor.
One-third of its members are elected by Local Authorities.
One-third of its members are elected by Members of the Legislative Assembly from among non-MLAs.
11.x: Option B is incorrect: the Governor nominates one-sixth of the Council, not one-fourth. Local authorities and MLAs each elect one-third, and MLAs choose from among non-members.
11.tq: Recall the Governor's share: one-sixth.
n: One-third of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by local authorities. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

The MLAs elect these members from among non-MLAs. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s:
Assertion (A): The State Legislative Assembly is a temporary and dissolvable body.
Reason (R): Its normal term is five years unless it is dissolved earlier.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
11.x: Both are true: the Assembly is temporary because its normal term is five years and it can be dissolved earlier. R explains A.

The State Legislative Assembly can be dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

n: The co-operative movement is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The co-operative movement is not a nomination ground for the Rajya Sabha under Article 80. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s: Which of the following statements regarding an ordinary Bill passed by a State Legislative Assembly is incorrect?
o: The total maximum period for which the Legislative Council can delay the Bill is four months.
The State Legislative Council may delay the Bill for a maximum of three months after its first passage.
After the Bill is re-passed by the Legislative Assembly, the Legislative Council may delay it for a maximum of one month.
The Legislative Council can permanently block an ordinary Bill passed by the Legislative Assembly.
11.x: Option D is incorrect: the Council has no veto and cannot block an ordinary Bill for good. It can delay the Bill for three months, then one month after it is passed again, four months in all.
11.tq: Look for the statement giving the Council a veto.
n: The Legislative Council has no veto power over ordinary bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill for a maximum of 3 months after its first passage. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

The Legislative Assembly can re-pass an ordinary bill after its first passage through the Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

11.s:

n: The Vice-President is not a member of the Council of States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

n: Municipalities are among the local authorities that elect members of a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
District Boards are among the local authorities that elect members of a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]

12.s: The office of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha is governed under which Part of the Constitution?
12.x: The Speaker's office is in Part V (the Union), mainly Articles 93–96, 100, 110 and 118. Part VI covers the States, where the Assembly Speaker sits.
12.tq: Discriminate Part V (Parliament) from Part VI (State Legislatures).
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is governed under Part V of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s: Who elects the Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
o: The Rajya Sabha from among its sitting members
The Prime Minister from among elected Lok Sabha members
The Lok Sabha from among its sitting members
The President from among all Members of Parliament
12.x: Under Article 93, the Lok Sabha elects its Speaker from among its own sitting members. Neither the President nor the Prime Minister chooses the Speaker.
12.tq: Recall who elects each presiding officer of Parliament.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The regular Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by Lok Sabha members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s: Which of the following statements regarding eligibility for election as Speaker of the Lok Sabha is incorrect?
o: Membership of the Lok Sabha is required at the time of election.
A non-member may be chosen as Speaker under the six-month relaxation rule.
The Speaker is elected from among the sitting members of the Lok Sabha.
The person must already be an elected Member of the Lok Sabha.
12.x: Option B is incorrect. There is no six-month relaxation for the Speaker, who must already be an elected Lok Sabha member when chosen. That relaxation applies only to Ministers.
12.tq: Discriminate the Minister's six-month rule from the Speaker's eligibility.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha must already be an elected Member of Parliament at the time of election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
A non-member cannot be chosen as Speaker under the six-month relaxation rule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s: With regard to the office of the Speaker, which statement is correct?
o: The Speaker takes oath solely as an ordinary Member of Parliament.
The Speaker takes oath before the Deputy Speaker as presiding officer.
The Speaker takes a separate oath as presiding officer.
The Speaker takes no oath as a Member of Parliament.
12.x: The Speaker takes no separate oath as presiding officer, only the oath taken as an ordinary MP. Options B and C invent an oath of office.
12.tq: Remember that presiding officers take no separate oath of office.
n: The Speaker takes no separate oath of office as presiding officer. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker takes an oath solely as an ordinary Member of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s: The Lok Sabha Secretariat functions directly under the control and guidance of the:
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
12.x: The Lok Sabha Secretariat works directly under the Speaker's control and guidance, not under the executive, which keeps the House independent.
12.tq: Recall who controls each House's secretariat.
n: The Lok Sabha Secretariat functions directly under the control and guidance of the Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s:

o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
12.x: Both are true: under Article 96, the Speaker cannot preside while a resolution for their own removal is considered, even if present. R gives the rule behind A.
12.tq: Recall the Article 96 bar on presiding.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 96. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s:
Consider the following statements:

12.x: Both are true: under Article 100, the Speaker does not vote in the first instance in normal sittings, but gives a casting vote when votes are tied.

n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 100. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

During normal parliamentary sittings, the Speaker exercises a casting vote under Article 100 upon an equality of votes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: During consideration of the Speaker's own removal resolution, the Speaker may speak and take part in the proceedings.
Statement B: During such consideration, the Speaker may exercise a casting vote in case of a tie.

Which of the following is correct?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
12.x: A is true: during their own removal, the Speaker may speak, take part and vote in the first instance. B is false because no casting vote is allowed then, the reverse of normal sittings.

During consideration of the Speaker’s own removal resolution, the Speaker is entitled to vote in the first instance like an ordinary member. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

(iii) Resigns to the Deputy Speaker

12.x: The Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker and the Deputy Speaker to the Speaker, under Article 94(b). The resignation goes sideways, not up to the President. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.

n: The Speaker addresses resignation in writing to the Deputy Speaker under Article 94(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Deputy Speaker addresses resignation in writing to the Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker’s resignation goes laterally to the Deputy Speaker rather than upward to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s: Which of the following statements regarding the effect of dissolution of the Lok Sabha is incorrect?
o: The Speaker continues until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Lok Sabha.
The Speaker continues in office after dissolution.
The Speaker does not vacate office immediately upon dissolution.
The Speaker's office ends immediately on the date of dissolution.
12.x: Option D is incorrect: the Speaker does not vacate office on dissolution but stays until just before the new Lok Sabha first meets.
12.tq: Recall the Speaker's continuity after dissolution.
n: When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Speaker does not vacate office immediately. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The regular Speaker continues in office through dissolution until the next House meets. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding removal of the Speaker:
I. Removal requires a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha.
II. The resolution requires at least 14 days' advance written notice.
III. Removal requires a simple majority of members present and voting.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
12.x: I and II are correct: under Article 94(c), the Speaker is removed by a majority of all the then members (an effective majority), after 14 days' notice. III is false because a simple majority is not enough.
12.tq: Discriminate effective majority from simple majority.
n: The Speaker is removed only by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha under Article 94(c). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The majority required to remove the Speaker is an effective majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
At least 14 days’ advance written notice is required before moving the Speaker’s removal resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

(iv) Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha
12.x: The Speaker presides over a joint sitting (Article 118(4)), then the Deputy Speaker, then the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman. Money Bill certification is under Article 110(4). The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
12.tq: Recall the order of who presides over a joint sitting.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 110. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s:
How many of the following functions or powers are specifically associated with the Speaker in the given list?
1. Adjourns the House in the absence of a quorum
2. Suspends sittings in the absence of a quorum
3. Exercises adjournment sine die
4. Fixes the date for election of the Deputy Speaker
12.x: All four belong to the Speaker: adjourning or suspending the House when there is no quorum (one-tenth, Article 100), adjourning sine die, and fixing the Deputy Speaker's election date under Rule 8(1).
12.tq: Check each item for whether the Speaker or the President does it.
n: The Speaker adjourns the House in the absence of a quorum. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker suspends sittings in the absence of a quorum. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The quorum is one-tenth of the House’s strength under Article 100. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker exercises adjournment sine die. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker fixes the date for the election of the Deputy Speaker under Rule 8(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s:
Assertion (A): The Speaker decides questions of disqualification of Lok Sabha members arising out of defection.
Reason (R): Such questions arise under the Tenth Schedule and the Speaker's decision is subject to judicial review as indicated in Kihoto Hollohan.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

n: The Speaker decides questions of member disqualification arising out of defection under the Tenth Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s: Under Rule 8(1), who fixes the date for the election of the Deputy Speaker?
o: The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

n: The Speaker fixes the date for the election of the Deputy Speaker under Rule 8(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

12.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the Regular Speaker and the Pro-Tem Speaker.

o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
12.x: A is true: by convention, the Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the senior-most member of the new House. B is false because the office ends as soon as the regular Speaker is elected.

12.s: Which of the following correctly describes a primary function of the Pro-Tem Speaker?

Administering oath to newly elected MPs and enabling election of the regular Speaker

The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 96. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 100. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 110. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]

14.s: Which of the following correctly describes the composition of Parliament?
o: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha only; the President is a member of both Houses
President and Lok Sabha only; Rajya Sabha is not part of Parliament
President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; the President is an integral part but not a member of either House
President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; the President is a nominated member of Rajya Sabha
14.x: Under Article 79, Parliament consists of the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. The President is part of Parliament but not a member of either House.
14.tq: Discriminate between being part of Parliament and being a member of a House.

14.s: An Ordinary Bill may be introduced in:
o: Either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha
14.x: An ordinary bill can be introduced in either House. Only Money Bills and Financial Bills under Article 117(1) must start in the Lok Sabha.
14.tq: Recall which bills must start in the Lok Sabha.

14.s: Which of the following statements about a Money Bill is incorrect?
o: It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha.
The prior recommendation of the President is mandatory for its introduction.
A Joint Sitting may be held if the two Houses disagree on it.
The Rajya Sabha can make recommendations within 14 days.
14.x: Option C is incorrect: there is no joint sitting on a Money Bill, because the Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days and the Lok Sabha decides. A Money Bill starts in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation.
14.tq: Recall the two kinds of bill excluded from joint sittings.

A Money Bill requires the President’s prior recommendation for introduction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha may make recommendations on a Money Bill only within 14 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Money Bill cannot be considered in a Joint Sitting. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Money Bill requires the President’s recommendation before introduction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Joint Sitting under Article 108 is not applicable to a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s:

Statement B: A Financial Bill under Article 117(3) can be introduced in either House, but the President’s recommendation is needed before consideration.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
14.x: Both are true: a Financial Bill under Article 117(1) starts only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation. One under Article 117(3) can start in either House, but needs the recommendation before it is considered.
14.tq: Discriminate recommendation for introduction (117(1)) from recommendation for consideration (117(3)).

A Financial Bill (I) may be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Financial Bill (I) requires the President’s recommendation for introduction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Financial Bill (II) is governed by Article 117(3). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

The President’s recommendation is required before consideration of a Financial Bill (II). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the effect of dissolution of the Lok Sabha:
I. A Bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses.
II. A Bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses.
III. A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha but not passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse.
IV. Prorogation causes every pending Bill to lapse.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
14.x: I, II and III are correct: on dissolution, bills pending in the Lok Sabha, or passed by it and pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapse, but a bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that the Lok Sabha never passed survives. IV is false because prorogation ends no bill.
14.tq: Trace which House each bill is pending in when the Lok Sabha dissolves.
n: A Bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that has not been passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
Prorogation does not cause a Bill to lapse. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s: Which of the following statements regarding State Legislature Bills is incorrect?
o: A State Money Bill originates in the Legislative Assembly.
The Legislative Council can delay an Ordinary Bill for a maximum of 6 months.
The Governor’s recommendation is required for the introduction of a State Money Bill.
The Legislative Council gets 14 days to consider a State Money Bill.
14.x: Option B is incorrect: a Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill for at most four months (three, then one), not six. A State Money Bill starts in the Assembly on the Governor's recommendation, and the Council has 14 days to consider it.

14.s:
How many of the following statements about a Constitution Amendment Bill are correct?
1. It may be introduced in either House of Parliament.
2. Prior recommendation of the President is not needed for its introduction.
3. A Joint Sitting may be held to resolve disagreement between the Houses.
4. It is passed by a special majority in each House separately.
14.x: Three are correct: an amendment bill can start in either House without the President's recommendation, and needs a special majority in each House separately. Statement 3 is false because there is no joint sitting for it.
14.tq: Recall that amendment bills have no joint sitting.
n: A Constitution Amendment Bill may be introduced in either House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed separately by each House by a special majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Constitution Amendment Bill cannot be passed through a Joint Sitting. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Constitution Amendment Bill does not require the President’s prior recommendation for introduction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Joint Sitting under Article 108 is not applicable to a Constitution Amendment Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s: A Private Member’s Bill is introduced by:
o: Any MP who is not a Minister
A Minister who is not a member of either House
14.x: A Private Member's Bill is introduced by any MP who is not a Minister, whether elected or nominated. A Minister's bill is a Government Bill.
14.tq: Discriminate between Private Member's and Government Bills.
n: A Private Member’s Bill is introduced by a Member of Parliament who is not a Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

14.s:

I. It is passed by a simple majority.
II. The Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha have equal legislative powers regarding it.
III. A Joint Sitting is possible in case of a deadlock.
IV. The Rajya Sabha has no fixed constitutional time limit to consider it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
14.x: All four are correct: an ordinary bill needs a simple majority, both Houses have equal powers over it, a deadlock can go to a joint sitting, and the Rajya Sabha has no fixed time limit on it.
14.tq: Contrast ordinary bills with the 14-day limit on Money Bills.

An Ordinary Bill is passed by a simple majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Joint Sitting is possible for an Ordinary Bill in case of a deadlock. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has no fixed constitutional time limit to consider an Ordinary Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s:

1. It may be introduced only in the Lok Sabha with the President’s prior recommendation.
2. It includes taxation and borrowing matters.
3. It includes the custody of, and withdrawal from, the Consolidated Fund.
4. A Bill dealing merely with fines or penalties is a Money Bill.
14.x: Three are correct: a Money Bill starts only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation and covers taxes, borrowing and the Consolidated Fund. Statement 4 is false because a bill only about fines or penalties is not a Money Bill (Article 110(2)).
14.tq: Recall the Article 110(2) exclusions.
n: A Money Bill may be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Money Bill requires the President’s prior recommendation for introduction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Money Bill includes provisions relating to taxes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Money Bill includes provisions relating to borrowings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Money Bill includes provisions relating to the custody of the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Money Bill includes provisions relating to withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Bill dealing merely with fines or penalties is not a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Money Bill requires the President’s recommendation before introduction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s: Under Article 110(3), whose decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill is final?
o: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
14.x: Under Article 110(3), the Lok Sabha Speaker's decision on whether a bill is a Money Bill is final. Neither the President nor the Rajya Sabha Chairman can overrule it.
14.tq: Recall who certifies Money Bills.
n: The Lok Sabha Speaker’s decision under Article 110(3) on whether a Bill is a Money Bill is final. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

I. It involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India.
II. It does not contain matters specified in Article 110.

14.x: All three are correct: a Financial Bill (II) involves spending from the Consolidated Fund but contains no Article 110 matter. It is treated as an ordinary bill, so a joint sitting is possible.

A Financial Bill (II) does not contain matters specified in Article 110. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding a Constitution Amendment Bill:
I. It cannot originate in a State Legislature.
II. Special majority means a majority of the total membership of the House plus two-thirds of the members present and voting.
III. Certain federal provisions require ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures.
IV. The President shall give assent to it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
14.x: All four are correct: an amendment bill cannot start in a State Legislature, needs a special majority (majority of total membership plus two-thirds present and voting), and federal changes need half the States. The President must give assent.
14.tq: Recall each step of the Article 368 procedure.
n: A Constitution Amendment Bill cannot originate in a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

The President shall give assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s:

2. An Ordinary Bill requires a simple majority.
3. A Money Bill requires a simple majority.
4. A Money Bill requires a special majority.
14.x: Three are correct: an ordinary bill needs no prior recommendation and passes by simple majority, and a Money Bill also passes by simple majority. Statement 4 is false because a Money Bill does not need a special majority.

An Ordinary Bill requires a simple majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Money Bill requires a simple majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s:
How many of the following statements regarding presidential action on Bills are correct?
1. The President may assent to an Ordinary Bill.
2. The President may withhold assent to an Ordinary Bill.
3. The President may return an Ordinary Bill once.
4. The President may assent to a Money Bill.
5. The President may withhold assent to a Money Bill.
6. The President cannot return a Money Bill.
14.x: All six are correct: the President can assent to, withhold or return once an ordinary bill. A Money Bill can be assented to or withheld but never returned.
14.tq: Discriminate the President's options on ordinary bills and Money Bills.
n: The President may assent to, withhold assent from, or return an Ordinary Bill once. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The President may assent to or withhold assent from a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The President cannot return a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding a Joint Sitting of Parliament:
I. A Joint Sitting under Article 108 is applicable to an Ordinary Bill.
II. The President expresses the intention to summon a Joint Sitting.
III. The Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides if the Lok Sabha Speaker is absent.
IV. The quorum for a Joint Sitting is one-tenth of the total membership.
V. The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha presides if both the Lok Sabha Speaker and Deputy Speaker are absent.

I, II, III, IV, V and VI
I, II, III and IV only
14.x: All six are correct: a joint sitting is for ordinary bills, called by the President, presided over by the Speaker (then the Deputy Speaker, then the Deputy Chairman), and has a quorum of one-tenth. It decides by simple majority.

A Joint Sitting decides questions by a simple majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s: What is the effect of a Joint Sitting having been notified by the President when the Lok Sabha is dissolved?

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

14.s: Regarding a Money Bill, which of the following correctly describes the role of the Rajya Sabha?

The Rajya Sabha may make recommendations on a Money Bill only within 14 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]

14.s: Under which Lok Sabha Rule is the No-Confidence Motion governed?
14.x: A no-confidence motion comes under Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha Rules, not the Constitution. Rule 184 is for a discussion with a vote, 377 for special mentions and 8(1) for the Deputy Speaker's election.

Rule 8(1) governs the procedure for the election of the Deputy Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 72-75]
The day-to-day proceedings of Lok Sabha are governed by the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 72-75]
The No-Confidence Motion is not mentioned in the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 72-75]

14.s:

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

14.s: Certiorari is described as a writ that is:
o: Curative and preventive, and may quash an order already passed
Issued to direct a public official to perform a mandatory duty
Only preventive and issued to stop an inferior court from exceeding jurisdiction
Issued to inquire into a person's claim to a public office
14.x: Certiorari is both curative and preventive: a higher court uses it to quash an order a lower court or tribunal has already passed without jurisdiction or in error of law. Prohibition is only preventive.

Statement A: Advice tendered by the Supreme Court under Article 143 is binding on the President in all cases.
Statement B: On pre-Constitution disputes, the Supreme Court is bound to give advice.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
17.x: A is false: advice under Article 143 does not bind the President. B is true: on references about pre-Constitution treaties and agreements (Article 143(2)), the Court must give its opinion.
17.tq: Discriminate Article 143(1) ('may') from 143(2) ('shall').
n: Under Article 143, the Supreme Court is bound to give advice on pre-Constitution disputes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Advice tendered by the Supreme Court under Article 143 is not binding on the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s: Which of the following statements regarding removal of a Supreme Court judge is incorrect?
o: The grounds are proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
Removal is made by an order of the President.
The procedure is governed by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
The removal address requires a simple majority in each House of Parliament.
17.x: Option D is incorrect: a judge is removed only after an address passed in each House by a special majority (majority of total membership plus two-thirds present and voting), not a simple majority. The grounds are proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
17.tq: Recall the special majority needed to remove a judge.
n: A Supreme Court judge is removed by an order of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The President issues the removal order after an address by Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Proved misbehaviour is a ground for removing a Supreme Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Incapacity is a ground for removing a Supreme Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Removal of a Supreme Court judge requires a special majority in each House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The special majority requires a majority of the total membership of the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The special majority requires at least two-thirds of the members present and voting. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The special majority must be obtained in the same session. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 governs the removal procedure procedurally. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Removal of a Supreme Court judge requires a parliamentary special-majority address under Article 124(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Removal of a Supreme Court judge requires a statutory inquiry. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s:
How many of the following statements are correct?
1. Under Article 129, the Supreme Court is a Court of Record.
2. The Court of Record includes the power to punish for contempt of itself.
3. Under Article 130, the seat of the Supreme Court is Delhi.
4. The CJI may decide another place with the President's approval.
17.x: All four are correct: under Article 129, the Court is a Court of Record with power to punish contempt. Under Article 130, its seat is Delhi, but the CJI may choose other places with the President's approval.
17.tq: Recall Articles 129 and 130.
n: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court to be a Court of Record. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Supreme Court has the power to punish for contempt of itself under Article 129. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 130 provides for the seat of the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The seat of the Supreme Court is Delhi. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Chief Justice may decide on other places for Supreme Court sittings with the approval of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s: Under which Schedule is the oath of office of the Chief Justice of India prescribed?
17.x: The forms of oath for the CJI and other judges are in the Third Schedule. Their salaries and privileges are in the Second Schedule.
17.tq: Discriminate the Second Schedule (pay) from the Third Schedule (oaths).
n: The oath of office of the Chief Justice of India is prescribed under the Third Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 124 concerns the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court.
II. Article 124(4) provides the removal procedure for Supreme Court judges.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Both are correct: Article 124 sets up the Supreme Court, and Article 124(4) gives the procedure for removing its judges.
17.tq: Recall the clauses of Article 124.
n: Article 124 concerns the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 124(4) provides the removal procedure for Supreme Court judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Appointment of an ad hoc Supreme Court judge
(b) Attendance of a retired judge at Supreme Court sittings
(c) Appointment of an Acting Chief Justice
(d) Removal of a Supreme Court judge
