i. President appoints the Acting Chief Justice when the Chief Justice is unable to perform duties
ii. Chief Justice appoints with the prior consent of the President
iii. Chief Justice requests attendance with the prior consent of the President
iv. President passes an order after an address by Parliament
17.x: The CJI appoints ad hoc judges and asks retired judges to sit, both with the President's consent. The President appoints an Acting CJI and orders removals after Parliament's address. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
17.tq: Discriminate what the CJI does from what the President does.
n: The Chief Justice appoints ad hoc judges with the prior consent of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Chief Justice requests retired judges to attend Supreme Court sittings with the prior consent of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s: Under which Article may the President refer questions of law or fact to the Supreme Court?
17.x: Under Article 143, the President can refer questions of law or fact to the Supreme Court for its opinion.
17.tq: Recall Article 143.
n: The President may refer questions of law or fact to the Supreme Court under Article 143. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The First Judges Case held that constitutional consultation did not mean concurrence.
II. The First Judges Case established executive supremacy in judicial appointments.
III. The Second Judges Case held that consultation meant concurrence and introduced the Collegium system, initially consisting of the Chief Justice of India and two senior-most Supreme Court judges.
IV. The Third Judges Case expanded the Collegium for Supreme Court appointments to the Chief Justice of India and four senior-most Supreme Court judges.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: All four are correct: the First Judges Case (1981) gave the executive primacy, the Second (1993) read consultation as concurrence and created a three-member collegium, and the Third (1998) enlarged it to the CJI plus four judges.
17.tq: Trace how the collegium changed from case to case.
n: The First Judges Case held that constitutional consultation did not mean concurrence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The First Judges Case established executive supremacy in judicial appointments. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Second Judges Case held that constitutional consultation means concurrence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Second Judges Case introduced the Collegium system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Collegium initially consisted of the Chief Justice of India and two senior-most Supreme Court judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Third Judges Case expanded the Collegium for Supreme Court appointments to the Chief Justice of India and four senior-most Supreme Court judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s:
Assertion (A): The National Judicial Appointments Commission was struck down as unconstitutional.
Reason (R): It was struck down to preserve the independence of the judiciary.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
17.x: Both are true: in 2015, the Supreme Court struck down the NJAC because it threatened the independence of the judiciary, which is part of the basic structure. R explains A.
17.tq: Ask whether the threat to independence explains the strike-down.
n: The National Judicial Appointments Commission was struck down as unconstitutional. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The National Judicial Appointments Commission was struck down to preserve the independence of the judiciary. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s:
How many of the following statements are correct?
1. Article 32 gives a fundamental right to approach the Supreme Court directly.
2. Article 32 enables direct approach to the Supreme Court for enforcement of Part III rights.
3. The Supreme Court exercises writ jurisdiction under Article 32.
4. Habeas Corpus is a writ issued under the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction.
5. Mandamus is a writ issued under the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction.
6. Prohibition is a writ issued under the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction.
7. Certiorari is a writ issued under the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction.
8. Quo Warranto is a writ issued under the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction.
17.x: All eight are correct: Article 32 is itself a fundamental right to go directly to the Supreme Court to enforce Part III. Under it, the Court can issue all five writs.
17.tq: Recall the five writs under Article 32.
n: Article 32 gives a fundamental right to approach the Supreme Court directly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 32 enables direct approach to the Supreme Court for enforcement of Part III rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Supreme Court exercises writ jurisdiction under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Habeas Corpus is a writ issued under the Supreme Court’s writ jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Mandamus is a writ issued under the Supreme Court’s writ jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Prohibition is a writ issued under the Supreme Court’s writ jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Certiorari is a writ issued under the Supreme Court’s writ jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Quo Warranto is a writ issued under the Supreme Court’s writ jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 143:
I. The Supreme Court may tender advice on a question of law or public importance.
II. The Supreme Court may refuse to tender advice on a question of law or public importance.
III. The Supreme Court is bound to tender advice on every question of law or public importance referred to it.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: I and II are correct: under Article 143(1), the Court may give or refuse its opinion on a question of law or public importance. III is false because it is not obliged to answer every reference.
17.tq: Discriminate 'may' (143(1)) from 'shall' (143(2)).
n: Under Article 143, the Supreme Court may tender advice on a question of law or public importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Under Article 143, the Supreme Court may refuse to tender advice on a question of law or public importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Ad hoc judge—required approval
(b) Ad hoc judge—required consultation
(c) Ad hoc judge—purpose of appointment
(d) Supreme Court judge—appointment authority and concurrence

List-II
(i) Previous consent of the President
(ii) Concerned High Court Chief Justice
(iii) Meeting a lack of quorum
(iv) President in consultation with the prescribed collegium concurrence

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
17.x: An ad hoc judge needs the President's prior consent, after consulting the High Court's Chief Justice, to make up a quorum. Regular judges are appointed by the President on the collegium's advice. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
17.tq: Recall the conditions for an ad hoc judge.
n: An ad hoc judge is appointed with the previous consent of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
An ad hoc judge is appointed after consultation with the concerned High Court Chief Justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
An ad hoc judge is appointed to meet a lack of quorum. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The President appoints Supreme Court judges in consultation with the prescribed collegium concurrence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Judgments of the Supreme Court have evidentiary value because the Supreme Court is a Court of Record.
Statement B: Judgments of the Supreme Court cannot be questioned when produced before a subordinate court.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
17.x: Both are true: as a Court of Record, the Supreme Court's judgments serve as evidence and cannot be questioned when produced before a lower court.
17.tq: Recall what being a Court of Record means.
n: Judgments of the Supreme Court have evidentiary value because the Supreme Court is a Court of Record. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Judgments of the Supreme Court cannot be questioned when produced before a subordinate court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Article 131 does not cover pre-Constitution treaties.
Statement B: Article 131 does not cover inter-State water disputes.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
17.x: Both are true: Article 131's original jurisdiction does not cover pre-Constitution treaties (its proviso) or inter-State water disputes (left to Article 262).
17.tq: Recall the exclusions from Article 131.
n: Article 131 does not cover pre-Constitution treaties. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 131 does not cover inter-State water disputes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s: Article 262 of the Constitution concerns which of the following?
o: Federal disputes under the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
Review of judgments and orders by the Supreme Court
17.x: Article 262 lets Parliament provide for settling inter-State water disputes and bar the courts from them. That is why Article 131 does not cover them.
17.tq: Recall Article 262.
n: Article 262 concerns inter-State water disputes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

17.s: The Supreme Court of India is governed under which Part, Chapter and range of Articles of the Constitution?
17.x: The Supreme Court is in Part V (the Union), Chapter IV, Articles 124–147. Part VI covers the States.
17.tq: Discriminate the Supreme Court's Articles (124–147) from the High Courts' (214–231).
n: The Supreme Court of India is governed under Part V, Chapter IV of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Articles 124 to 147 deal with the Supreme Court of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s: The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on:
17.x: The Supreme Court was inaugurated on 28 January 1950, two days after the Constitution came into force on 26 January.
17.tq: Discriminate 28 January 1950 from 26 January.
n: The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on 28 January 1950. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Supreme Court succeeded the Federal Court of India.
The Supreme Court succeeded the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
The Supreme Court succeeded the Council of States established under the Government of India Act, 1935.
The Federal Court was established under the Government of India Act, 1935.
17.x: Option C is incorrect: the Supreme Court replaced the Federal Court (set up under the 1935 Act) and the Privy Council's Judicial Committee. The Council of States is the Rajya Sabha, not a court.
17.tq: Recall the two courts the Supreme Court replaced.
n: The Supreme Court of India succeeded the Federal Court of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Federal Court of India was established under the Government of India Act, 1935. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court of India succeeded the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: A Supreme Court judge retires at the age of 65 years.
Statement B: A Supreme Court judge may be removed by the President following an Address supported by a Special Majority in each House of Parliament on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
17.x: Both are true: a Supreme Court judge retires at 65 (Article 124(2)) and is removed by the President after an address passed by a special majority in each House for proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Article 124(4)).
17.tq: Recall the retirement age and the removal process.
n: Supreme Court judges retire at 65 years of age under Article 124(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The President removes Supreme Court judges after an Address supported by a Special Majority in each House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Proved misbehaviour is a ground for removing a Supreme Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Incapacity is a ground for removing a Supreme Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

Match List-I with List-II:

(b) Writ jurisdiction
(c) Review jurisdiction
(d) Advisory jurisdiction

List-II
(i) Article 137
(ii) Article 143
(iii) Article 131
(iv) Article 32
17.x: Original jurisdiction is Article 131, writs Article 32, review Article 137, and advisory opinions Article 143. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
17.tq: Recall the Article for each kind of jurisdiction.
n: The Supreme Court has original and exclusive jurisdiction under Article 131. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has writ jurisdiction under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has review jurisdiction under Article 137. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction under Article 143. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s: Which of the following statements regarding the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131 is incorrect?
o: It includes recovery of damages by a private party against the Union.
It excludes inter-State water disputes under Article 262.
It covers disputes between one State and another State.
It covers direct federal disputes involving a legal right between the Centre and one or more States.
17.x: Option A is incorrect: Article 131 covers only disputes about legal rights between the Centre and States or between States. A private party suing the Union for damages goes to the ordinary courts.
17.tq: Recall that Article 131 applies only between governments.
n: The Supreme Court has original and exclusive jurisdiction under Article 131. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 covers direct federal disputes involving a legal right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can hear under Article 131 disputes between one State and another State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 excludes inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover recovery of damages by a private party against the Union. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can hear under Article 131 disputes between the Centre and one or more States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s:
Assertion (A): The Supreme Court cannot refuse an Article 32 petition.
Reason (R): Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
17.x: Both are true: the right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself a fundamental right, so the Court cannot turn away an Article 32 petition. R explains A.
17.tq: Ask whether being a fundamental right explains why the Court cannot refuse.
n: The Supreme Court cannot refuse an Article 32 petition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s: Which of the following writs is included in the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 32?
17.x: Under Article 32, the Court can issue habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. Review, advisory opinions and special leave are other kinds of jurisdiction.
17.tq: Discriminate the five writs from other kinds of jurisdiction.
n: The Supreme Court has writ jurisdiction under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can issue the writ of Habeas Corpus under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 32 directly enforces Fundamental Rights.
Statement B: The Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction is broader than that of the High Courts under Article 226.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
17.x: A is true: Article 32 enforces fundamental rights directly. B is false because High Courts' writ power under Article 226 is wider, covering legal rights as well as fundamental rights.
17.tq: Discriminate Article 32 (fundamental rights only) from Article 226 (other rights too).
n: Article 32 provides direct enforcement of Fundamental Rights in Part III. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is narrower than that of the High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 226 empowers High Courts to enforce Fundamental Rights and legal rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court's power to grant Special Leave to Appeal is:
o: Discretionary and available against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal, subject to the stated exception
Mandatory and limited to High Court judgments
Advisory and limited to presidential references
Available only in civil proceedings involving a constitutional question
17.x: Under Article 136, the Court may, at its discretion, grant special leave to appeal against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal, except military tribunals (Article 136(2)).

n: The Supreme Court has discretionary appellate power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s:
Assertion (A): The Supreme Court's review jurisdiction under Article 137 is distinct from judicial review of statutes.
Reason (R): Article 137 concerns the power of the Supreme Court to review its own judgments or orders.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
17.x: Both are true: Article 137 lets the Court review its own judgments, which is why it differs from judicial review of laws. R explains A.
17.tq: Discriminate review of a judgment from judicial review of a law.
n: The Supreme Court has review jurisdiction under Article 137. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to review its own judgments or orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Review jurisdiction under Article 137 is distinct from judicial review of statutes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s:
Assertion (A): An opinion rendered by the Supreme Court to the President under Article 143 is not binding on the President.
Reason (R): Under Article 145(3), a reference under Article 143 must be heard by a bench of at least five judges.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
17.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: an Article 143 opinion is advisory and does not bind the President, while the five-judge bench rule of Article 145(3) only fixes who hears the reference.
17.tq: Ask whether creating a jurisdiction explains that its opinions are non-binding.
n: The Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction under Article 143. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Opinions rendered by the Supreme Court to the President under Article 143 are strictly advisory. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 143 opinions are not binding on the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Under Article 143(1), the President may refer questions of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court.
II. Under Article 143(1), the Supreme Court may tender its opinion.
III. Under Article 143(2), the Supreme Court must tender its opinion on pre-constitutional matters.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: All three are correct: under Article 143(1), the President may refer questions of public importance and the Court may give its opinion. Under 143(2), it must give one on pre-Constitution matters.
17.tq: Discriminate 'may' (143(1)) from 'must' (143(2)).
n: The President can refer questions of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion under Article 143. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Under Article 143(1), the Supreme Court may tender its opinion on matters of public importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Under Article 143(2), the Supreme Court must tender its opinion on pre-constitutional matters. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

(ii) Article 145(3)

19.x: Dicey's book was 1885, A.K. Gopalan 1950, Kesavananda 1973 and Maneka Gandhi 1978. The order is A, B, C, D.

After Maneka Gandhi in 1978, due process of law requires a law to be just, fair, and reasonable. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

19.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Dicey’s third principle and its position in India?
o: Dicey’s third principle concerns the primacy of individual rights.
In the United Kingdom, the Constitution is described as the result of judicial decisions on individual rights.
India adopted Dicey’s third premise without modification.
In India, the Constitution is the source of rights.
19.x: Option C is incorrect: India took Dicey's first two elements but reversed the third. In India, rights come from the Constitution, not the other way round.
19.tq: Remember how India departs from Dicey's third element.
n: Dicey’s third classic element of the Rule of Law is the primacy of the rights of the individual. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Dicey’s third element states that the Constitution is the result of individual rights defined and enforced by courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Dicey’s third element treats individual rights as resulting from judicial definition and enforcement rather than as originating from the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
In the United Kingdom, the Constitution is the result of judicial decisions on individual rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
In India, the Constitution is the source of rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
India reverses Dicey’s third premise while adopting Dicey’s first two principles intact. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

19.s: Executive discretion without objective standards or judicial safeguards is regarded as what under Article 14?
o: A prerequisite for Rule of Law
19.x: Executive discretion without objective standards or safeguards is arbitrary and therefore violates Article 14.
19.tq: Remember that arbitrariness violates Article 14.
n: Executive discretion without objective standards is ultra vires Article 14. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Executive discretion without judicial safeguards is ultra vires Article 14. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

19.s: The Rule of Law was borrowed into the Indian constitutional system from which source?
19.x: India borrowed the rule of law, along with parliamentary government and the writs, from the British constitutional system.
19.tq: Recall what India borrowed from Britain.
n: The Indian Constitution borrowed the Rule of Law from the British Constitutional System. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

19.s:

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

19.tq: Ask whether opposing special tribunals explains equal subjection to law.

19.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Public Interest Litigation promotes access to justice for disadvantaged persons.
II. Public Interest Litigation is an indispensable prerequisite for the existence of the Rule of Law.
III. The Rule of Law existed before the evolution of Public Interest Litigation.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
19.x: I and III are correct: PIL widens access to justice for the disadvantaged, and the rule of law existed before PIL through Articles 14, 32 and 226. II is false because PIL is not a precondition for the rule of law.
19.tq: Discriminate what strengthens the rule of law from what is required for it.
n: Public Interest Litigation promotes access to justice for disadvantaged persons. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Public Interest Litigation strengthens access to justice for disadvantaged persons. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Public Interest Litigation is not an indispensable prerequisite for the existence of the Rule of Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law existed before the evolution of Public Interest Litigation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law existed through Articles 14, 32, and 226 before the evolution of Public Interest Litigation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

List-I

(b) Article 21
(c) Article 32
(d) Article 226

List-II
(i) Text associated with Procedure Established by Law
(ii) Constitutional anchor of the Rule of Law

(iv) High Court writs for Fundamental Rights and other legal rights
19.x: Article 14 anchors the rule of law, Article 21 contains 'procedure established by law', Article 32 gives the Supreme Court writ power for fundamental rights, and Article 226 gives High Courts wider writ power. The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
19.tq: Recall what each Article provides.

II. Dicey’s second element places everyone above ordinary law.
III. Dicey’s third element concerns the primacy of individual rights.

19.x: I and III are correct: Dicey's first element rejects arbitrary power and the third gives individual rights primacy. II is false because the second element puts everyone under the ordinary law, not above it.

19.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect about the concepts included in the Rule of Law?
o: No person can be punished except for a distinct breach of established law.
No one is above the law under the equality principle.
People’s responsibility to the Government is a pillar of the Rule of Law.
Regular law has predominance over arbitrary power.
19.x: Option C is incorrect: people's duty to the government is not part of the rule of law, which restrains the government. The other options state Dicey's elements correctly.
19.tq: Find the item that reverses the aim of the rule of law.
n: The first element requires the absolute supremacy or predominance of regular law over arbitrary power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

People’s responsibility to the Government is not a pillar of the Rule of Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

19.s:
How many of the following statements are consistent with the Rule of Law?
I. Government is subordinate to law.
II. Laws should be just, fair and non-arbitrary.
III. The ruler remains above the law.
IV. Executive discretion should operate without objective standards.
19.x: Two are consistent with the rule of law: government bound by law, and just, fair laws. A ruler above the law and discretion without standards belong to 'rule by law'.
19.tq: Discriminate 'rule of law' from 'rule by law'.
n: Rule of Law means that the government itself is subordinate to the law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Rule of Law requires laws to be just, fair, and non-arbitrary. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Rule of Law represents government under law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

The Rule of Law restrains the government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

19.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Article 14 applies to citizens.
Statement B: Article 14 applies to foreigners.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
19.x: Both are true: Article 14 protects 'any person', so it covers foreigners as well as citizens, unlike Articles 15, 16 and 19, which are for citizens only.
19.tq: Discriminate rights for any person from rights for citizens only.
n: Article 14 applies to citizens. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]

20.s: Under which Article is the Governor appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal?
20.x: Under Article 155, the President appoints the Governor by warrant under hand and seal. Article 153 provides a Governor for each State, 156 the term, and 159 the oath.
20.tq: Recall Articles 153 to 159 in order.
n: The President appoints the Governor under Article 155 by warrant under the President’s hand and seal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The President appoints the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]

20.s: Which of the following statements regarding the qualifications of the Governor is incorrect?
o: The person must have completed 35 years of age.
The person must be a citizen of India.
The person should not hold any office of profit.
The person may continue as a member of Parliament after becoming Governor.
20.x: Option D is incorrect: a Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature, and must give up any such seat on appointment. They must be a citizen, at least 35, and hold no office of profit.
20.tq: Recall the Governor's qualifications under Articles 157 and 158.
n: The Governor must be a citizen of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor must have completed 35 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor must not be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
A person appointed as Governor must vacate a parliamentary or State Legislature seat held by that person. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor must not hold any office of profit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]

20.s:
Assertion (A): The normal term of office of a Governor is five years, but the Governor may leave office earlier or continue longer.
Reason (R): The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
20.x: Both are true: the Governor's term is five years, but they hold office during the President's pleasure (Article 156), so they can be removed earlier or stay on until a successor takes over. R explains A.
20.tq: Ask whether the President's pleasure explains the flexible term.
n: The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President under Article 156. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The normal term of the Governor is five years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor can be removed before completing the normal term of five years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]

The Governor’s term is five years subject to the pleasure of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President, not the Chief Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]

20.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The emoluments and allowances of the Governor are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
II. If the same person is Governor of two or more States, the salary is shared in the proportion determined by the President.
III. The oath of the Governor is administered by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: All three are correct: the Governor's emoluments are charged on the State's fund, a Governor of two States is paid in shares the President fixes, and the High Court's Chief Justice administers the oath (Article 159).
20.tq: Recall who swears in the Governor and how pay is shared.
n: The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court administers the Governor’s oath under Article 159. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The emoluments and allowances of the Governor are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State under Article 202. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
When the same person is Governor of two or more States, the President determines the proportion in which the salary is shared. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The same person can be appointed as Governor of two or more States under the Seventh Amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]

(d) Article 213

List-II

20.x: Article 153 provides a Governor for each State, 154 vests executive power in them, 159 covers the oath, and 213 ordinances. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
